attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: A firm present-tense description. It keeps the concession that systems work better, the word 'often' and the lab-versus-real-world contrast. The next sentence's 'probably' is a separate claim and is correctly left out.

contract.note: Reading 'superficial' as practical unreliability and 'often' as recurring failure is an ordinary, fair plain reading. January 2023 and the population of systems were chosen by the evaluator, as the contract flags. The contract also fairly requires evidence beyond one selected product.

evidence.note: CNET's own account of its January 2023 audit: AI-assisted articles needed corrections and use was paused. This partly supports recurring real-world failure, but it covers one in-house tool and mixes model errors with editing errors.
A 2022 OpenAI evaluation showing InstructGPT is more reliable than GPT-3. It bears on the conceded improvement, not on how often deployed systems failed in January 2023.

reviews.rationale: The only outcome evidence is one company's account of one in-house tool, and it does not separate model errors from editing errors. The contract asks for evidence across systems and ordinary uses, and the packet does not provide it. Nothing contradicts the claim, but the evidence does not settle it either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence. He cites the named works but makes the claim in his own voice.

semantics.note: Revision 2 correctly restores 'some of' and 'help establish'. 'Help establish' limits the claim to a contribution of evidence; it is not a probability hedge, so the claim stays a scorable observation.

contract.note: The contract takes the modest reading, that the named works contribute evidence that some old limitations persist. That is fair. Using 2022 and the list of example limitations are the evaluator's choices, as the contract flags. Requiring that both named works be checked fits the speaker's attribution.

evidence.note: Fodor and Pylyshyn (1988) document the earlier debate about systematicity and compositionality. It is historical background only.

A 2022 PNAS abstract finds compositional generalization elusive for standard networks but captured by a modified neural model. This is partial and mixed persistence evidence, and it does not address Mitchell or Stochastic Parrots.

reviews.rationale: Neither named work was recovered in usable form, so the contribution Marcus attributes to them cannot be verified. The one 2022 study gives narrow, mixed evidence on persistence. The packet does not meet the contract's support condition or its contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own tweet, embedded and endorsed in his post. The Alexandr Wang quote below it is not Marcus's claim.

semantics.note: The 2020s line is captured. The 1980s comparison comes from the first line of the same tweet and is his own analogy; the contract rightly treats it as an analogy that is not scored.

contract.note: Reading 'vast' as substantial spending across the industry on human feedback and correction work is fair. The contract flags that 'vast' has no threshold and that the company population is unspecified. It rightly excludes Wang's forecast as evidence.

evidence.note: TIME reports a company-stated figure of about $150k for one OpenAI–Sama partnership. That is one contract, not an industry total, and it gives no budget context for judging 'vast'.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no industry-wide spending total and no budget context for 'vast'. A single small contract value neither establishes nor rules out vast spending across the industry. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in the PS of his post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps his stated uncertainty about how much has changed and treats the outsourcing-to-sweatshops point as the firm assertion. That is faithful.

contract.note: It reads 'sweatshops' as outsourced work under poor conditions and 'handcrafting' as an analogy that covers labeling. Both are ordinary readings. January 2023 and how far the shift must go are the evaluator's choices, as the contract flags.

evidence.note: Semafor (January 2023) reports that OpenAI outsourced about 1,000 contractors to create training data. This supports the outsourcing part only, not poor conditions and not a shift away from graduate-student work.
Guardian, August 2023: Kenyan moderators allege poor conditions on Sama's OpenAI work in 2021–22. This is outside the target month, the allegations are disputed, and it is not true counterevidence.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows outsourcing of training-data work in January 2023. It does not show poor working conditions for that workforce in the period, and it does not show the claimed shift away from graduate-student work. The support condition is only partly met and nothing contradicts the claim.
